Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty;
recorded by his disciple Guanding.
The Bodhisattva precepts are the opening chapter for mobilizing goodness and the vanguard for repelling evil;
by returning directly to the Way, the source of birth can be exhausted.
If even the Śrāvakas of minor practice cherish and revere the Prātimokṣa,
how could a Mahāsattva, who possesses a broader vision, not maintain the categories of precepts with diligence?
Both the internal and external paths alike honor and uphold them.
The common people of the royal house have surrendered themselves with reverent devotion;
this is indeed the supreme cause for attaining the ultimate fruit and the wondrous karma for establishing the site of enlightenment.
However, the characteristics of the precepts recorded in the sūtras and śāstras are of many kinds,
and the methods for receiving them as explained in the biographies and commentaries are not without their similarities and differences.
This is truly because the capacities and insights of sentient beings vary— whether partial or complete— such that they require either detailed or concise teachings.
Words are not duplicated and matters do not proceed in parallel.
Now, I have carefully examined the Dharma characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) as set forth by Master Śīkṣānanda;
they originate from the *Vinayapiṭaka-vastu-saṃgrahaṇī* of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.
In the third year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, Master Shi arrived within the borders of Han territory.
He brought forth the illumination of the Mahāyāna and rectified the holy teachings,
translating over three hundred fascicles of sūtras and śāstras.
This single volume of the Brahmajāla Sūtra was chanted forth at its conclusion as a vow for its wide propagation;
therefore, I have reverently recited each word three times,
especially because its literary expressions and meanings are obscure and its underlying intent is profound and mysterious.

As for why the sutra is titled the *Brahmajāla*: [The text continues: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the Palace of the Fragrant Terrace, preaching the Dharma for his mother, Queen Mahāmāyā. At that time, the Buddha, having completed ninety days of summer retreat, descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī. Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard that the Buddha had descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately went to the Buddha’s presence and said to him: ‘World-Honored One, when you were in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for your mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, you did not entrust this Dharma to anyone. Now that you have returned to Jambudvīpa, whom shall you entrust with this Dharma? The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘I have already entrusted this Dharma to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, hearing the Buddha’s words, immediately went to the place where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was and said to him: “Mañjuśrī, the Buddha has entrusted this Dharma to you. Mañjuśrī replied: “Ānanda, what Dharma does the Buddha wish me to receive? Ānanda said: “The Buddha wishes you to receive the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Mañjuśrī asked: “What is the *Brahmajāla*? Ānanda replied: “It is the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Mañjuśrī said: “If it is called the *Brahmajāla*, then I shall receive it. Ānanda said: “Mañjuśrī, the Buddha has entrusted this Dharma to you. You should now receive it. Mañjuśrī said: “Ānanda, I am now receiving it. Having spoken these words, he immediately rose from his seat and went to the Buddha’s presence. To clarify that the Buddha-dharmas of the various Buddhas differ like the mesh of the net of Brahmā,
this chapter speaks of the "ground of the mind."
The bodhisattva’s ethical discipline universally guards the three types of action.
Mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are one in essence, though they have different names.
Among these three types of action, mental action is primary, while bodily and vocal actions are secondary.
Based on the ultimate perspective, it is called the "Mind-Ground" (Cittabhūmi).
This precept sūtra is explained through three layers of profound meaning (*xuan-yi*).
First is the explanation of the name.
The second [section] clarifies the essential nature;
the third provides a detailed analysis.
Within the explanation of the name:
First, the names of the persons are clarified;
next, the titles of the teachings are distinguished;
finally, the stages and ranks are elucidated.
In the Indian Sanskrit language, it is *mahābodhisattva*;
now, when we speak of "Bodhisattva," we have abbreviated the remaining characters. Translated, it means: [Great Being of Enlightenment].
The Great Path-mind accomplishes sentient beings;
it is also called the "Opening Being" (Bodhisattva) and the "Great Courageous Mind."
Furthermore, it is called "Excellence" (Kalyāṇa).
It is named according to its practice;
because its mental application is vast and universal, this title was established on that account.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that this person possesses the mind of the Great Way,
which is indestructible like a diamond (*vajra*).
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of equal awakening,
all are called Bodhisattvas; they are also referred to as "Sons of the Buddha."
To succeed and continue is its essential meaning.
Since all three vehicles arise from the Buddha,
the exhaustion of delusions constitutes the meaning of being a "son."
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"If one were like my own son,
a Mahāsattva would be superior in terms of succession."
They are called true children.
Furthermore, all three vehicles equally cultivate the path;
this principle applies to them all.
The two vehicles, from their own realization down to their minor fruits, are narrow and short-lived;
the Great Being, however, is vast and long-lasting, as he realizes his own path and enables others to do so—
hence he receives this title.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* on the Arousing of the Resolve states:
"From the very beginning, he has been the Teacher of Gods and Humans,
surpassing both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
Therefore, it is called the "Great Mind.
Next, the designation of the dharma is explained as having the meaning of "precept" (śīla);
in the Sanskrit language, it is *śīla*.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
"In the language of Qin, it means 'inherently good' (xing shan);
it is also called 'cool and refreshing' (qing liang)."
Because it can stop the heat and affliction of breaking the precepts,
it is named according to its function; it is also called *pratimokṣa*.
Translated as "Preserving Liberation.
Also named "Pure Livelihood," and further described as "Accomplishing Dignified Conduct and Not Accepting or Storing Possessions."
In future births, one will be free from the three evil realms and receive a physical form in a pure land;
being able to cease wrong livelihood and prevent wrongdoing while stopping evil is also called "precept" (śīla).
This is an explanation of the meaning based on its etymological significance.
Furthermore, the statement that "le" (勒) means "restraint" (禁) is likewise a name established according to its semantic function.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"If you still speak of impermanence despite the Buddha’s prohibition,
you violate the Buddha’s precept and your tongue shall fall away."
Furthermore, it is said:
"All the precepts observed by such a person are incomplete;
they cannot even attain the bodhi of the two vehicles."
How much more so regarding the unsurpassed path!
Now, as for what is called "precept" (śīla),
there are the precepts of restraint (saṃvara-śīla), the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (dhyāna-sahabhū-śīla), and the precepts concurrent with the Path (mārga-sahabhū-śīla).
This name originates from the Tripiṭaka.
"Vinaya" (律) means prohibition; "vyañjana" (儀) refers to physical deportment.
It is that which can restrain all evils within one's physical conduct.
Therefore, it is called "precept" (śīla) and is also termed "dignified deportment" (īryāpatha).
"Dignity" (wei) means being pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring.
Ritual is the standard of conduct;
the practitioner is solemn and awe-inspiring.
It is also called "Taming and Governing."
It causes the activities of the mind to become disciplined and wholesome.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is stillness and gathering;
at the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes disciplined and wholesome, preventing all evils.
The Way is that which enables passage.
Once true realization has been attained, one naturally refrains from transgressions;
for instance, when a practitioner of the first fruit plows a field, the insects remain four inches below the surface.
This is the power associated with the Path.
Since these two types of precept-dharma are superior mental forces,
they are able to give rise to the path of precepts and meditative concentration, arising simultaneously with the restraint of discipline (saṃvara).
Therefore, it is called "shared.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
there are the vows of restraint, the vows of meditative concentration, and the untainted vows.
Although these names originate from the Tripiṭaka,
the bodhisattva precepts likewise possess these three aspects.
That which is obtained through formal vows is called restraint (*saṃvara*).
If a bodhisattva’s [vows] are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*),
they all cease the three types of karma and are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*). If they comprise the restraint of the code (*saṃvara-śīla*), [they are so called].

The three categories of ethical discipline (śīla) are: the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas, the discipline of gathering sentient beings, and the discipline of restraining misconduct. These are the names of the three clusters of ethical discipline.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the great being’s discipline (*mahāsattva-saṃvara*) encompasses both the cessation and the engagement of the three karmas. Here,
because it is manifested through both body and speech, it is collectively termed "discipline."
Regarding the gathering of virtue:
based upon the vows of restraint, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment;
this enables one to cease all non-virtuous actions and diligently cultivate all forms of virtue.
This fulfills the vow for enlightenment.
Regarding "gathering in sentient beings," there are eleven matters by which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings.
All of these serve to benefit things and extensively profit sentient beings.
Having extensively enumerated all the bodhisattva precepts within the Chapter on Precepts,
it is concluded that the nine types of precepts are all subsumed within the three precepts.
The vows cause the mind to abide;
by gathering what is wholesome, one accomplishes the Buddha-dharma for oneself,
and by gathering sentient beings, one brings them to maturation.
These three encompass all the precepts of a Mahāsattva.
The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states:
"The precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the ten *pārājika* offenses."
"Comprising the wholesome" refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
"Comprising sentient beings" refers to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
it means transforming and reaching out to sentient beings so that they may attain peace and happiness.
In the "Chapter on Precepts" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, ten kinds of precepts are enumerated:
first, the unimpaired;
second, the unbroken.
Third, not piercing;
fourth, not mixing;
fifth, following the path.
Sixth, non-attachment;
seventh, praised by wisdom;
eighth, mastery.
Ninth, following meditative concentration;
tenth, fulfillment.
One should infer the meaning from these ten.
"Without deficiency" means maintaining the natural precepts and the naturally grave precepts with purity,
as if guarding a bright jewel.
If one violates [the precepts], one is like a vessel that has already been broken;
such a person is a mere peripheral follower of the Buddha-dharma.
One who does not violate them—
To maintain these thirteen [rules] without breach or damage:
"not piercing" refers to the *pāyattika* offenses and so forth.
If one commits transgressions, it is like a vessel with holes or leaks;
such a person is incapable of receiving the Way.
As for "not being defiled":
If one maintains the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration, yet while maintaining that discipline brings to mind matters of breaking the precepts,
it is called "mixed."
Through meditative concentration, the mind is sustained such that sensual thoughts do not arise.
A Great Sūtra says:
"To engage in verbal jesting and mockery."
The sound of bracelets outside the wall;
men and women pursuing one another—
all these defile the pure precepts.
"Following the Path" means that by conforming to the principle of the Truths (satya), one is able to destroy the afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
"Unattached" means...
Seeing the truth constitutes becoming a noble one;
thus, one is not defiled by the afflictions of discursive thought.
These two points concern the observance of the precepts according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The morality praised by the wise,
the morality of mastery,
and the morality that involves a bodhisattva’s transformation of others for the sake of buddhahood are what is praised by the Buddha.
One attains mastery within the world;

this refers to the observance of the precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). In accordance with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is fully endowed with both types of precepts.
This is precisely following the Śūraṅgama Samādhi to manifest various dignified postures without arising from the samādhi of cessation,
displaying the forms of the ten dharma realms to guide and benefit sentient beings;
though these postures arise and move, they are spontaneously and eternally pure.
Therefore, it is called the morality that accords with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). As for the various types of morality mentioned previously,
they are termed "incomplete" because their restraint is merely through formal discipline (*saṃvara*).
The precepts of the Middle Way lack no precept that is not complete;
therefore, they are called "fully endowed.
By means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, one universally enters into all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "complete.
This is the upholding of the precepts of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
Next, the stages [of practice] are explained.
The various teaching gates expounded by Śākyamuni Buddha throughout his single career of transformation,
when investigated according to their underlying meaning, clearly comprise the four teachings:
namely, the Tripitaka, the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* cites the Kātyāyanīya-vibhaṅga to clarify the limits of the six perfections:
Śibi’s substitution of himself for the pigeon was the fulfillment of dāna;
King Sumati’s avoidance of falsehood was the fulfillment of śīla.
The Rishi Kṣāntivādin was unmoved when King Kali cut out his heart; this was the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
The Great Giver (*Mahādānapati*) drained the ocean; this was the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Śāṇakavāsin [protected] a bird's nest; this was the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Guvā, Pin, and the Great Minister divided the lands to settle disputes;
these were Bodhisattvas whose wisdom was perfected. This is clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
There are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds in a manner corresponding to sarvajñā (all-knowledge);
these are bodhisattvas who have attained penetration. There are also bodhisattvas...
He resolves his mind to sport with supernatural powers and purify Buddha-lands.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*,
he manifests through the inconceivable liberation, transforming his body and ascending the seat.
Furthermore, those who again undergo humiliation and reprimand are distinct bodhisattvas; upon generating the resolve,
they immediately sit at the site of enlightenment and achieve perfect awakening.
Turning the Wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings is the perfection of the Bodhisattva.
Among the four types of Bodhisattvas:
The depths and stages of practice shall now be explained.
The Three Piṭakas primarily concern the Hīnayāna;
among the Śrāvakas, there are seven types of noble beings (ārya).
There are three types of external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*):
first, the five stabilizing practices (*pañca sthāpanā*); second, the distinct-characteristics applications of mindfulness (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī smṛtyupasthāna*).
Third is the general mindfulness foundation (smṛtyupasthāna).
Next, one enters the stage of the inner ordinary person (pṛthagjana), wherein there are four roots of goodness (kuśalamūla);
the fourth is the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Fifth, the stage of the summit;
sixth, the stage of patience;
seventh, the stage of the supreme mundane dharma.
Beyond this, one enters the stage of the noble ones (ārya):
first, the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin);
second, the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin).
Third, those with faith and understanding;
fourth, those who have attained through vision; fifth, those who have realized it through the body.
Sixth, those liberated at specific times;
seventh, those liberated independent of time.
Such are the śrāvakas.
For a bodhisattva, regardless of their stage, there is no severing of afflictions; they simply cultivate the six perfections.
If one discusses the sequence of stages, it can only be compared to the Lesser Vehicle in terms of depth and shallowness.
From the first arousal of the mind of enlightenment, one gives rise to the vow of compassion and contemplates the Four Noble Truths.
Taking the Truth of the Path as the primary gateway, one single-mindedly cultivates the six perfections:
through *dāna* (generosity), one destroys the realm of hungry ghosts and rescues those in the hells.
With patience, one rescues the animals;
with diligence, one uproots the asuras;
with meditative concentration, one brings peace to human beings.
The Wisdom-Illumination Heaven hosts,
from Śākyamuni to Kanakamuni and Kaśyapa, constitute the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa;
therein they attain five kinds of merit.
First, one will not be reborn in the three evil realms;
second, one will not be born in a frontier region;
third, one’s sense faculties will be complete and intact.
Fourth, they shall not receive a female body.
Fifth, they shall constantly remember their past lives,
yet they themselves will not know whether or not they will become Buddhas.
The position of "corresponding observation" (*zhǔnwàng*) refers to the specific and general foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
From the time of Śikhin until Dīpaṃkara, it is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
During that period, although he knew within himself that he would become a Buddha, he did not speak of it aloud.
The position of "approximate observation" (*quanwang*) lies within the stage of the nature of the Dharma of Warming (*uṣmagata*).
Since one already possesses faith in the realized Dharma,
one will certainly know that by practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), one will become a Buddha.
The mind was not yet clear, so he did not speak of it to others.
From the time of Dīpaṃkara until Vipaśyin, the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas were fulfilled.
At that time, his inner mind clearly knew for himself that he would become a Buddha, and he spoke these words aloud.
The state of "alignment at the summit" lies within the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmāvasthā*).
By practicing the six perfections and clarifying the understanding of the four truths,
one is like someone who, having ascended a mountain peak, perceives clearly in all four directions.
Therefore, he speaks to others with his mouth.
If one has planted the karma for the thirty-two marks over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*,
this may be estimated as being the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
If one sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) while established in the stage of "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti),
one enters into reality in the subsequent single moment;
through thirty-four moments of mind, one severs the fetters and attains perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
This constitutes Buddhahood.
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the Bodhisattvas follow the ten stages common to the Three Vehicles.
The first is the Stage of Dry Wisdom (Ganhuedi).
The phenomena and their names are identical to those of the Tripitaka;
however, the mental states of contemplative practice differ.
In essence, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are like illusions and transformations.
The collective refutation of the eight inversions of views and attachments is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The same applies to the mind, feelings, and phenomena (*dharmas*).
One dwells within this contemplation.

Although one has not yet attained the "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) dharma— the water that accords with the principle— one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path,
because the wisdom of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is profound and sharp.
This is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi).
Second, the Stage of Nature (gotra-bhūmi) refers to having transcended the Stage of Dry Wisdom.
Having attained the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata),
one is able to progress through the initial, middle, and final moments of mind to enter the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan) and even up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma);
all these are termed the "Stage of Nature" (gotrabhūmi).
It is called the "Stage of Nature" (dharmatā-bhūmi) because one has attained the water of the untainted nature (anāsrava-dharmatā).
Third is the "Stage of the Eight Persons," which consists of those who practice through faith and those who practice through the Dharma within the three vehicles.
By realizing that phenomena are merely provisional, one gives rise to the true and severs delusions.
Within the Uninterrupted Samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*), the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are fully perfected;
because wisdom is yet lacking by one part, this is called the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*).
Regarding the fourth stage, the Ground of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*):
the practitioners of the three vehicles equally perceive the principle of the first meaning— the Four Noble Truths as non-arising—
and equally sever the delusions of view, exhausting all eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Fifth is the Stage of Thinness (Tanubhūmi).
Its essence is that conventional love gives rise to the realization of the ultimate;
by severing the afflictions of the desire realm, one realizes the sixth liberation.
The afflictions are attenuated.
Regarding the six stages of detachment from desire:
the substantial craving of the three vehicles is, when provisional, identical to the real.
Because one has severed the five lower fetters of the desire realm— namely, the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual greed, and ill-will—
it is called the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*). Seventh is the stage of those who have already accomplished their task (*kṛtāvibhūmi*).
For those of the three vehicles, when the craving for form and the formless is realized as emptiness, the outflow-free state truly arises;
they sever the five higher fetters: restlessness, conceit, doubt, attachment to form, and attachment to the formless.
The seventy-second [stage] exhausts all matters and delusions within the three realms;
hence it is called the Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*).
The eighth is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddha gives rise to true, outflow-free [wisdom];
